meta.subtitle:
The family tree of the fifteen shoguns of Edo
and the heads of the house since 1868

ieyasu.name: Tokugawa Ieyasu
ieyasu.title: Shōgun
ieyasu.bio: Eldest son of Matsudaira Hirotada, lord of Okazaki, he was appointed shogun in 1603 and passed the office to Hidetada in 1605, ruling on as ōgosho. He destroyed the Toyotomi at Osaka in 1614–15, died at Sunpu in 1616 and was deified as Tōshō Daigongen.

saigo.name: Saigō no Tsubone
saigo.bio: Ieyasu's consort and the mother of Hidetada and Tadayoshi. Born in 1562 by the Nihon Jinmei Daijiten; other sources give 1552.

hidetada.name: Tokugawa Hidetada
hidetada.title: Shōgun
hidetada.bio: Ieyasu's third son, he arrived late at Sekigahara and angered his father. After handing the office to Iemitsu in 1623 he kept real power as ōgosho until his death.

iemitsu.name: Tokugawa Iemitsu
iemitsu.title: Shōgun
iemitsu.bio: Born in Edo Castle in 1604 and raised by his wet nurse Kasuga no Tsubone, he reigned through the Shimabara Rebellion (1637–38) and the 1639 ban on Portuguese ships that completed the closed-country system.

ietsuna.name: Tokugawa Ietsuna
ietsuna.title: Shōgun
ietsuna.bio: He became shogun as a boy in 1651, with his uncle Hoshina Masayuki assisting him in government.

tsunayoshi.name: Tokugawa Tsunayoshi
tsunayoshi.title: Shōgun
tsunayoshi.bio: Lord of Tatebayashi and adopted heir of his elder brother Ietsuna, he is known for the Laws of Compassion for Living Things, which earned him the name “dog shogun”, and for the Genroku cultural flowering.

ienobu.name: Tokugawa Ienobu
ienobu.title: Shōgun
ienobu.bio: As Tsunatoyo, lord of Kōfu and grandson of Iemitsu, he was adopted by Tsunayoshi in 1704 and reigned only three years.

ietsugu.name: Tokugawa Ietsugu
ietsugu.title: Shōgun
ietsugu.bio: Shogun from the age of three (four by Japanese count), he ruled through Manabe Akifusa and Arai Hakuseki and died as a child without an heir, so the succession passed to the Kii house.

yoshimune.name: Tokugawa Yoshimune
yoshimune.title: Shōgun
yoshimune.bio: Fourth son of the lord of Kii and lord of Kii himself from 1705, he was the first shogun from one of the three senior branch houses and led the Kyōhō reforms (1716–45).

ieshige.name: Tokugawa Ieshige
ieshige.title: Shōgun
ieshige.bio: Sickly and hard to understand, he was said to be intelligible only to his chamberlain Ōoka Tadamitsu.

ieharu.name: Tokugawa Ieharu
ieharu.title: Shōgun
ieharu.bio: On his father's dying advice he relied on Tanuma Okitsugu.

ienari.name: Tokugawa Ienari
ienari.title: Shōgun
ienari.bio: Adopted by Ieharu from the Hitotsubashi house, he reigned fifty years, the longest of any shogun, and kept real power as ōgosho after retiring in 1837. He is known for fathering 55 children.

ieyoshi.name: Tokugawa Ieyoshi
ieyoshi.title: Shōgun
ieyoshi.bio: He appointed Mizuno Tadakuni to carry out the Tenpō reforms (1841–43) and died just after Perry's arrival in 1853.

iesada.name: Tokugawa Iesada
iesada.title: Shōgun
iesada.bio: Too sickly to govern, he left affairs to Abe Masahiro, received the American consul Townsend Harris in 1857 and died during the dispute over his successor.

tenshoin.name: Tenshō-in
tenshoin.bio: Born into the Shimazu of Satsuma and adopted by its lord, Shimazu Nariakira, and by the Konoe court family, she married Iesada in 1856. In 1868 she worked with Kazunomiya to save the Tokugawa house and spare Edo Castle from attack, and afterwards raised the young Iesato.

show.sub: 1836 – 1883 · from Satsuma; pleaded for the house, 1868

iemochi.name: Tokugawa Iemochi
iemochi.title: Shōgun
iemochi.bio: Brought in from the Kii house as a boy, he married Emperor Kōmei's half-sister Kazunomiya in 1862 to bind court and shogunate together, and died at Osaka Castle in 1866 while his army was losing.

kazunomiya.name: Kazunomiya
kazunomiya.bio: A daughter of Emperor Ninkō and half-sister of Emperor Kōmei, she was married to Iemochi in 1862 to bind the imperial court and the shogunate together. In 1868 she petitioned the new government to spare the Tokugawa house and delay the army's advance on Edo, which helped the castle to be handed over without a fight.

yoshinobu.name: Tokugawa Yoshinobu
yoshinobu.title: Shōgun
yoshinobu.bio: A son of the Mito lord Nariaki, he headed the Hitotsubashi house before becoming the last shogun; in 1867 he returned governing power to the court. He lived until 1913 and was made a prince in 1902.

iesato.name: Tokugawa Iesato
iesato.bio: A Tayasu son, he succeeded Yoshinobu as head of the house in 1868 as a child of four and was President of the House of Peers from 1903 to 1933.

iemasa.name: Tokugawa Iemasa
iemasa.bio: A diplomat, he was the last President of the House of Peers (1946).

tsunenari.name: Tokugawa Tsunenari
tsunenari.bio: Son of Iemasa's daughter Toyoko, he took the Tokugawa name as his grandfather's heir and led the house for sixty years, founding the Tokugawa Kinen Zaidan in 2003.

iehiro.name: Tokugawa Iehiro
iehiro.bio: Tsunenari's eldest son, he became the 19th head of the house on 1 January 2023.

d_ietsugu_yoshimune.note: Succeeded from the Kii house; whether Ietsugu formally adopted him is disputed.

d_yoshinobu_iesato.note: Named head of the house in 1868, when Yoshinobu retired.

d_yorifusa_nariaki.note: Yorifusa → Yorishige (lord of Takamatsu) → … → Munetaka (from the Takamatsu line, adopted by Tsunaeda) → Munemoto → Harumori → Harutoshi → Nariaki. The 3rd and 4th lords, Tsunaeda and Munetaka, were adopted from the Takamatsu branch, so the line runs through Yorishige rather than through Mitsukuni.

d_munetake_yoshiyori.note: Tayasu heads: Munetake, Harusato, Narimasa, Naritaka, Yoshiyori; several were adopted. Narimasa was a son of Hitotsubashi Harusada and Yoshiyori was Narimasa's son, so by birth Yoshiyori and Iesato descend from Harusada; the line shows the headship of the Tayasu house.

n_iemitsu.text: Raised by his wet nurse Kasuga no Tsubone (1579–1643), who later ran the Ōoku, the women's quarters of Edo Castle.

n_ieyasu.text: Born on the 26th day of the 12th month of Tenbun 11, usually given as 1542; in the Western calendar this is January 1543.

n_tsunayoshi.text: His mother Keishō-in (1627–1705), a consort of Iemitsu, was by one account a Kyoto greengrocer's daughter.

n_yoshimune.text: Succeeded when the line of Hidetada died out with Ietsugu; whether Ietsugu formally adopted him just before dying is disputed.

n_nariaki.text: Mito lords between Yorifusa and Nariaki: Mitsukuni, Tsunaeda (Mitsukuni's nephew, adopted), Munetaka, Munemoto, Harumori, Harutoshi, Narinobu. Nariaki succeeded his brother Narinobu.

n_masako.text: Entered the palace in 1620 and became empress consort in 1624; her daughter reigned as Empress Meishō.

n_tsunenari.text: Whether Iemasa formally adopted him is not confirmed.

n_iesada.text: His first two wives died young; his third was Atsuhime (Tenshō-in), married 1856.

panels.intro: In 1603 Tokugawa Ieyasu was appointed shogun, and for 265 years his descendants ruled Japan from Edo. When the main line failed, heirs came from the branch houses Ieyasu and his successors had founded: the Kii, Hitotsubashi and Mito houses each supplied shoguns. In 1867 the last shogun returned power to the emperor; the head of the house today is the nineteenth.
caveats: Notes on uncertain points. Japanese sources date events in the lunar calendar; years here are Western years, which differ for a few people born late in the lunar year (Ieyasu, Ieshige, Tadanaga, Hoshina Masayuki, Tenshō-in, Matsudaira Sadanobu) or who died late in it (Tokugawa Mitsukuni). Reigns run from the imperial appointment to resignation or death.

From the fifth shogun on, most came to power by adoption, several from a branch house. Solid lines show birth; the crowns give the order, and the succession table says how each came to rule. Tsunenari's adoption by his grandfather is not confirmed in the sources used.
sources: Sources. Japanese reference works as published on Kotobank (Nihon Daihyakka Zensho, Yamakawa Nihonshi Shōjiten, Sekai Daihyakka Jiten, Nihon Jinmei Daijiten, Britannica Japan); Keiō University and nippon.com (2023) for the present heads. Draft: to be checked against Totman (1967) and the Cambridge History of Japan.
